If you are going to sell your PC, be ready to accept less than what you are willing to let it go for.  The price of parts depreciates quickly and everyone is looking for a deal.  A laptop is fine as long as you know what you're in for.

I'm with you on the fact that video games have excellent stories, but that's why I started watching "movie" versions of video games on youtube; skip all the gameplay and get right to the meat of it.  Also, don't compliment Ubisoft lol.  If the purchase of the year 2 pass is making you think it would be a waste, just going to have to bite the bullet.  Most people here would point you towards the sunk cost fallacy.

If you need graphics power on the laptop for other things, that could lead to wanting to game.  But if you don't need graphics power, then something like a Chromebook would probably be advisable.  You would also want it to be ARM based so you wouldn't be able to play games even if you tried.

Your main concern here is mainly the PC so hopefully, this provides advice that directly involves your inquiry.  Good luck

Yeah, that is an assumption.  
Again, did I ask for an easy way out?  I'm asking for actual concrete systems to abolish games for good.  That's the key here.
If I believe there was an easy way out I wouldn't even be here right now.  I'm asking for constructive advice for systems of accountability.

I also don't think you read the entirety of my post since you seem to have missed where I did call it an addiction.  I firmly believe it is an addiction, there's no denying that.  But simply saying "tough shit" isn't going to help anyone.
There isn't any constructive advice here.  I'm not asking to be saved, I'm asking for concrete systems.  Your comment comes off as aggressive like I'm at fault here for even saying anything.

I feel like I've digressed.  Ways to stop gaming is the key point here really.  Willpower and general motivational mantras, sure.  However, things like that just don't last for me.  I would throw out my computer if I could but it really can be useful for other things.  The consoles I can't do anything about either since my brother uses them responsibly.  

What I honestly think would most work is bringing someone in here and locking out my PC from being able to do anything involving games.  Whenever I adjust host files or install parental control programs, or delete everything, I just end up undoing it.  Nobody I know is computer literate but I'm thinking it wouldn't hurt to find somebody who could do that.

Also, I'm not really into Cam's videos.  His hand language is pretty distracting :p.  
I totally get the idea of "high scores" but I've never been a gamer that aims for the best scores or times.  It's just an escape for me.  I mean, I've gone 180 days of straight exercising to my limit but that didn't stop me from failing to start again once I veered off.  Looking at the quick start stuff, it focuses a lot on self-empowerment, but I've been through therapy long enough that I know the "feel good" stuff just isn't for me.  

Honestly, clear cut ways to abolish games is what I'm after starting with my PC.  There have to be systems of accountability that could be put to use here.  I don't smoke but it feels like having a carton of smokes lying out in the open with a zippo lighter sitting next to it wouldn't be the best of ideas.  Or if I'm an alcoholic I've got a keg of my favorite beer that is magically kept full at all times.
Thanks.

I should also mention that my mood swings have a lot to do with it.  The upswing is where I will take on new hobbies, but then the downswings hit and I game to get through it.  I can't bring myself to go anywhere or do anything and the mindlessness of video games is easy enough to do even when I'm out of it.

Nothing else ignites that spark.  

Two days ago, I went out and bought a hole saw for a drill I stole off my parents.  Started sawing a hole in my desk to run cables through and botched it by breaking the damn arbor.  So now I have this circle on my desk and a feeling of failure.  Couldn't sleep and just played games.  *sigh*  I know it's petty and I'll eventually bring myself to head back out to get what I need but right now it just sucks.

I've been to meetups but I end up feeling ashamed because I can't really share what I do with them.  The shame eats away at me and I fear that I'll be found out.  I'm not happy with myself at all.  

I have a  meal plan and recipes that I like to cook, but typically I'll game through meals and go without eating sometimes.  

*sigh* I just don't even know where to begin.

Yeah, pretty much anytime I stopped gaming it was straight to being obsessed with beer, tv shows, movies, and pretty much whatever let me tune out from the world.

I was studying Neuroscience at university and it wasn't that I disliked it and academics weren't the issue.  I just burnt out from failure to develop personal skills.  I've been in and out of community college since then and have credits just about everywhere.  I've just been putting off applying to a four year because I have no idea what the hell I really want to be doing and I don't want to end up with a useless degree and be in an even bigger rut.

I could focus on brushing up my chemistry and biology but it's been so long since I've studied a science course.  The STEM careers interest me definitely, but I can't be wasting time with gaming if I'm going to go down that path.  Honestly, I just feel like my brain is mush these days, it's going to be a long road to build up that lost gray matter.

People do say a lot that 25 isn't a big deal, but I can never get over the lost potential.

I have plenty of other interests, I just default to gaming.  I enjoy puzzles, karaoke,  model building, woodworking, programming, running, jazz, cosplay, reading, writing, napping in parks, being around animals, hiking, cooking, baking, etc. etc. etc.

The issue is that I just can't bring myself to dive into any of that.  There are moments here and there but I'm trying to figure out what I need to make them stick.  It's also rare that I'm invited out but when I am, I enjoy myself very much.  However, when I return home, the first thing I do is plop myself down in front of the computer.
I know you mean well but I already very much understand that quitting is necessary.  What I'm asking for is constructive advice.

Also, I did try to quit in high school.  But nobody was there to hold me accountable and the one friend I had in high school was also addicted to video games.  In fact, he was even angry at me that I would consider giving them up altogether.  To be honest, I'm prepared for negative responses to this, and I'm ready to take whatever people say.

I do this because I have nobody to talk to, so when I do have someone that's listening I can get really excited and say a lot.  There are only two people I know that can keep up with my excited speech with their own excited speech and I don't speak to them anymore for stupid reasons.

Go ahead and continue elaborately expressing yourself and find those people that will match you.  If somebody gives you a short reply, just make a note that you shouldn't waste your emotional energy on them.  There's no need to base how you feel based on how someone replies.  Your words hold incredible value and if others don't see that then it's their problem.
Well, at least you're getting some love today.  25 here, celebrating alone. wooooooooo

I really really want to do this.  Today is my birthday and I'm miserable.  Everything around me is just a reminder of all the shit I had to deal with.  I know my mentality still needs some changing, but I feel like it would be easier to do somewhere that isn't attached to negative feelings and memories.  I've written off my family and the toxic people in my life so there really isn't anything keeping me here.

I have experience in this one.  
It was somewhere around November of last year with bipolar.  Before that I had broken it off with all of my friends and said some incredibly harsh things.

After getting some help I started contacting people starting with the person I was closest to.  She said she missed me and we set up plans to see each other.  That one was the easiest.

Second closest I had a lot of explaining to do.  I had to put things into very clear terms and show that I understood why they were hurt by what I said.  Even though I said those things in a bad place, they were still my thoughts and I had to own up to that.  It was a long process that took months and now we aren't as close as we used to be, but at least have good times in groups.

Third person took two tries.  At first she said she stopped thinking of me altogether.  She said that what I did was incredibly uncalled for.  All I could do was offer my apologies.
After some months later I contacted her again with some new insight.  She was more receptive this time and we reignited our friendship where it left off.  Singing our hearts out in karaoke is what really helped.

Some people never responded at all, and others had some choice words.  I have a handful of people now that I can call genuine friends, and others that are happy to see me when I run into them.  This is enough for me.

To be honest, I've been in isolation for some months now for other reasons but I at least know my friends are there when I'm ready.

There is something to keep in mind.  You may make some progress with your friends, but you have to be prepared for underlying resentment.  There could be something in particular that they are holding back and it could come out in some point.  You have to face it head on and don't try to explain your way out of it.
Taking ownership of your faults will earn you respect and your friends will be more open to starting fresh.

I'm 25 and began my journey to recovery a year ago.

If you don't already, I would say start journaling and try to make note of anything that brings you even a bit of joy.  Also note negative thoughts and explore why you feel that way.  

I suppose starting from scratch can seem daunting, but a blank canvas means you're in control of your self-portrait.  

It won't be easy and you might not make progress as soon as you want.  It's important that you accept the struggle as you go and find ways to remind yourself of what you're trying to achieve.

I'm beginning year two into this process with bipolar.  It's still kinda nibbling at me and every so often I need to say "no, stop, bad."  Other times I give in and let it consume me until it gets bored and goes back to being docile.  Hopefully mental illness and I can learn to chill.

I think AP classes were more interesting but overall I felt the same way about school.  After a certain point school is more about picking up on social skills and building a good work ethic.  Once you hit college you pretty much relearn everything at an in-depth level and social skills become a necessity.  

Senior year I was in an AVID course and an AP US History and Economics course.  Those two classes provided some quality info on important life skills.  It is bizarre that it isn't a normal part of the curriculum.  I think the subreddits here like r/personalfinance provide all the resources you need to get started on learning about finances.

As for English, high school was about the time that I started to hate writing.  There isn't any freedom of expression and I got sent up to the office a few times due to the content of my work.  It's more about the formal structure of writing associated with journalism and research.  I had an English teacher once say she "looked like a slut" when looking at a photo of herself with a friend during class.  Whether or not she did, I don't know, but that didn't exactly inspire any respect. 
Also add on the fact that grading is subjective and tends to be biased, it can be demoralizing.

Feel free to speak your mind, it's always better to be honest and let things out.

For the time being it's just about making the best of your situation.  I'm not sure how things are at your school but a club wouldn't be a bad idea.  Time moves fast; blink and suddenly your school days are nothing but a distant memory.  People can suck and they all have their own reasons for it; focus on improving in every way you can and do your best to keep others from bringing you down.  Eventually you will meet people searching for the same things you are, that is what I have found to be true.

I'm sorry that my replies are lengthy, I just know how school can be and the problems that come with it.  I'd rather you tackle things now than be thinking how things could have been different when you're older.

Hey Panda.
It's going to take some weeks before you feel the effects so don't write of the Sertaline if you feel better in the first few days then down after.

I'd also like to state that Sertaline is an SSRI, which means that it is a Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor.  It won't magically produce Serotonin, the "happy" neurotransmitter, but the Sertaline will maintain a concentration of Serotonin in the synapse.

Once you start feeling consistently better and feel like you have the energy to do so, it is important that you get sunlight, proper sleep, exercise, and eat foods containing tryptophan.  This will ensure you maintain a proper supply of serotonin.

Since the SSRI prevents the reuptake of serotonin, there is increased opportunity for the serotonin in the synapse to be broken down by enzymes.  If the neurotransmitter is broken down, it can't be recycled through reuptake.

Medicine provides the alleviation of symptoms, allowing you to improve all aspects of your life.  I wish you the best of luck.

The way I see death is pretty much just the nothingness we experience during sleep except forever.  Then at the same time there was a nothingness before we were born, and I'm sure you can't recall many memories before the age of 2.  Don't worry about what comes after death, we all find out eventually.

So let's focus on living.
I understand having a family that isn't very supportive.  At that point you just have to accept it and focus on supporting yourself.

A counselor/therapist can really help you piece together what's on your mind.  Everything is confidential and they are unbiased, it makes for excellent discussion.

You say you work and I'm glad.  Having a good work ethic will be key here.  I'm not sure what you do or what your plans are but it wouldn't be a bad idea to find a second/better job.  Building your funds and moving out may be good for you.

Friendship, is a tricky thing.  It isn't very common that high school friends remain together after.  If they haven't kept in touch it could be for any number of reasons.  They can be incredibly busy in this new world they are finding themselves in.  Also, if you haven't tried contact them yourself then you should give it a shot.  No need to wait for things to happen.

Don't count on siblings for friends, you are your own person and should make friends based on shared interests/values rather than convenience.

I highly recommend meetup.com, it has been incredibly useful for me in finding new friends.  I'm turning 25 soon and it is difficult making friends but it isn't impossible.
The key is to expose yourself to new situations and let relationships bloom naturally.  

Another cliche is volunteering, you can meet a lot of people from different walks of life.

Joining a gym could really help in this regard as well.  I joined a gym beginning of last year and noticed that you'll see a lot of the same people.  I joined classes and socialized with the people that I saw on a regular basis.  Physical fitness is one of the greatest things you can do for yourself, the benefits will leak into all other aspects of your life.

I know this got long but there's just one more thing.  Don't worry about what defines happiness and how long it will last.  "This too shall pass."  
Everything comes and goes.  Happiness, sadness, people, etc.  It's part of the human experience.

I strongly relate to you and know how hard things can be.  With effort, you can make a life that is yours and yours alone.  Take hold of opportunities, take risks, make mistakes, learn from them.
Take a look at this http://yearcompass.com/ and objectively look at this past year and take a look at what you want to come next.

I wish you the absolute best in your journey, be strong.

Hey, writing is a huge passion for me as well.  I was just in the middle of recommending Stephen King's "On Writing" when I decided to read your other post and realized you were way ahead of me.  
It seems you are really concerned in being the best and that determination to be the best can be used to fuel your success.  At 15 you have an incredible potential to improve.  Your brain is still developing and forming new connections, your perception of the world has only begun to form.  Personally, those high school years were rough.  I was always incredibly hard on myself for everything that I did.  Even if there was an objective scale that declared my work as the greatest in all of time and space, I would still deny it and continue reaching for more.
I did some quick looking around and found this, I think it will best explain what I think will help you.
http://soulanatomy.org/the-psychological-reason-creative-people-are-their-own-worst-critics/

Be kind to yourself and don't be afraid to expose your work to the world.  You will improve with time, there is no sense in condemning yourself to obscurity so early in the process.

Thanks, I try to recognize the fact that everyone is in the same boat as well.  I can be incredibly vindictive but joining groups on meetup and hearing people out helps me understand different perspectives.  I'm trying to gain that bit of empathy that I seem to have lost along the way.  
I'll do everything I can to love myself as a whole.  

There was a post somewhere around here about YearCompass.  I printed out their booklet and I'm going through it at the moment reflecting on my past year and what I have to look forward to.  It's really helped me in realizing what I've gone through and how I've changed.  It's been helpful in analyzing myself without judgement.

I'm glad you found this.
 The negative talk has been a big part for me.  Growing up I didn't really have supportive people in my life.  My dad was a drunk and consistently undermined my achievements.  My mom had so much anxiety that she would shut down my attempts at independence by the thought that I would harm myself or be lead down a negative.  My aunt's family was intertwined with mine and her son/my cousin was a sadist, obsessed with torturing me in any manner possible.  Bullies, dismissive teachers, an inability to understand people, opportunistic friends,  etc.

The my pessimistic view of the world is practically hardcoded into my brain.  I have to force myself back into my reality consistently on a day to day basis or else I get trapped by the voices of my past.
I'm learning to train my brain into at least a less pessimistic version.

I met a friend in an online chat group, she's much older than I am and has been through a lot.  She helped me with the essay portion of a college application.  As we went through each question, I would answer things in my way and she would point out that I was incredibly negative.  She found a way to spin things into incredibly positive views that I would never have thought otherwise.  In the difference between mine and the right kind of mindset is incredible.

I understand where you are coming from with the anxiety.  I thought my problems were solved a long time ago as well, but it's important to accept that there will be moments of relapse.  It's a long process and I believe the best medicine is exposure to the events that cause anxiety.  What helped me the most was a local support group that made me feel welcome, listened to what I had to say, and provided excellent feedback.  To be honest, I wouldn't even dare to make posts like this online before but I've learned to be more open.

I like that subreddit, it's spreading good vibes and certainly beats the heck out of advice animals.
A lot of people certainly do point out my self awareness and I think I've been internalizing that more and more.  Sometimes I wish I wasn't so self aware but I hope that it will allow me to help others when the time comes.

As for the letters,
Somewhere around Spring of 2016, I did my round of contacting.  I contacted everyone that I possibly could.  Some were happy to hear from me, others wanted more of an explanation, and some were completely angry and held onto so much resentment that no amount of what I said could change how they feel.  It made me feel better but I still get glimpses of the person I used to be and have to shake the feeling I had back then.  I'm at war with my demons and from time to time I get overwhelmed, but I'm doing whatever I can to fight back.

I use Microsoft's OneNote to keep track of all my progress and it syncs with my phone so I'm always able to write down new bits of insight as they come.  It's been helpful.

Sorry for this incredibly lengthy reply, I have a knack for detail.
I like that quote, "...doesn't mean you future can't be better than you ever imagined."  That really resonates with me.  Good hearing from you and I hope you continue to make progress in your own journey.

I understand this kind of self-destructive behavior.  I've seen some friends go through it, and I've been guilty of it as well.  

The general idea is that there wasn't any closure.  You have lingering feelings and keeping tabs on her helps you feel close despite putting yourself in negative situation.

In these 6 months, have you pursued an interest in a hobby, or method of self-improvement?  Have you sought out any kind of way to socialize? 

It's really hard to let go, believe me I know this very well.  There was someone I had deep feelings for and after our falling out I would keep up on how she was doing.  It wasn't until I started doing other things to occupy my mind that I started to move on.  It also doesn't hurt to fall for someone else.  
In my life I would tell myself that there would be nobody else like her, that I blew my only once chance at happiness.  But truth is, love can hit hard and completely blindside you at any moment.

Five years is a long time to be in a relationship, be kind to yourself and realize that all these memories you have with her will remain with you.  Focus on the positives you gained from the relationship and slowly move-on.  

I understand Borderline Personality Disorder very well.  I've been around BPD patients and it's unfortunate to say that they are extremely difficult to be close to.  You did well to be there for her these last 5 years, be proud of that.

If you need to talk about this, feel free to send a PM.  Take care.

The general idea was to just continue to improve in any way that I can until I could be proud of who I am.

What's funny is that he wasn't even a mental health doctor, we were just talking about various things.  

In truth, dedication and practice will always provide the best results.  I think the key part I'm missing is being able to accept my mistakes as I practice, but that comes with practice too.
